title: Peer Review & Collaboration with Other Researchers

subChunks.title: Peer Review & Collaboration with Other Researchers

storyBeats.txt: Research done in isolation is research that goes unchallenged, Theodora said. And unchallenged research is research that accumulates errors invisibly. The peer review process exists precisely to make errors visible before they propagate.

Genealogists, as a community, have been slower to adopt peer review than many other historical disciplines. The tradition of private family research, the lack of institutional frameworks, the absence of mandatory accreditation — all of these have made genealogy a field where errors can persist for generations in published trees.

Professional genealogy is changing this. The NGSQ, the Genealogist, and the journals of county genealogical societies are peer reviewed. BCG portfolios are reviewed by panels. Society of Genealogists seminars invite critical discussion. These are all peer review, however informal.

And collaboration — working with other researchers who hold complementary knowledge — multiplies your effectiveness. You cannot know everything. The researcher in the Family History Centre who has spent forty years on a specific county may see in your data what you have missed.

subChunks.hookHtml:
Genealogical research is frequently presented as a solitary pursuit: one person, one family, one archive. In reality, the most productive and reliable genealogical work is increasingly collaborative. Regional societies pool knowledge of local records. One-name studies aggregate global instances of a surname. Forensic genealogy teams divide large tree-building tasks. DNA matching communities build shared reference data.

And peer review — the structured critical evaluation of research by qualified colleagues — is the mechanism by which errors are identified, methods are scrutinised, and conclusions are validated before they become embedded in the published record. Understanding how to engage with peer review, both as an author seeking critique and as a reviewer providing it, is a professional competency.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Forms of Peer Review in Genealogy

Peer review in genealogy takes several forms:

  • Journal peer review: Articles submitted to the NGSQ, The Genealogist, Genealogy (MDPI), and major county society journals are reviewed by editors and/or anonymous expert reviewers before acceptance. The standard is high: reviewers check methodology, citation quality, evidence analysis, and the soundness of conclusions.
  • BCG portfolio review: Applications for the Certified Genealogist credential are reviewed by panels of credentialled genealogists. Each portfolio item is assessed independently by multiple reviewers; discrepancies trigger discussion.
  • Society and study group critique: Many genealogical societies run 'brick wall' sessions, writing workshops, and research critique groups where members' work is reviewed by peers in a structured setting.
  • Informal peer review: Seeking a second opinion from a trusted colleague before publishing or submitting work. Less formal but widely practised.

Being Reviewed: What to Expect

Submitting work for peer review requires intellectual humility — the ability to receive criticism constructively. Common review comments include: insufficient citation; missing negative evidence; unresolved conflicts glossed over; conclusion language overclaiming the evidence; unfamiliarity with relevant secondary literature; and failure to consider alternative explanations.

The appropriate response to a peer review comment is not defensiveness but engagement: does the comment identify a genuine gap or error? If yes, correct it. If the reviewer has misunderstood, explain clearly. If the reviewer is wrong, make the case with evidence. Review correspondence should be professional, not personal.

Reviewing Others' Work

Providing peer review is itself a professional skill. Effective reviewers: focus on methodology, evidence, and citation rather than style; identify specific problems with specific citations or arguments rather than making general criticisms; distinguish between fatal flaws (that invalidate the conclusion) and improvements (that would strengthen the work but are not essential); are constructive, not hostile; and maintain confidentiality about the reviewed work.

Genealogists who serve as peer reviewers for journals or BCG portfolios must declare conflicts of interest (e.g., if the research concerns their own family). Blind review (where the author's identity is concealed) is standard in journal contexts; BCG portfolio review is not blind, as the portfolio requires demonstrated personal competency.

Collaboration with Other Researchers

Collaborative genealogical research takes many forms: one-name studies (Guild of One-Name Studies); surname DNA projects (FamilyTreeDNA); county or regional research groups; forensic genealogy teams; academic-genealogist partnerships (connecting professional genealogists with historians and demographers); and informal networks of mutual assistance among researchers with overlapping interests.

Effective collaboration requires: clear division of research responsibilities; agreed citation and documentation standards; explicit agreements about credit and publication rights; regular communication; and a shared understanding of quality standards.

Credit and Attribution

Professional ethics require that research contributions are properly attributed. If a colleague provides a key finding that enables your conclusion, cite them. If you use someone else's research as a starting point, cite it and give credit. Passing off others' research as your own — whether from a published source or from a private communication — is plagiarism, which violates the APG and BCG codes of ethics.

Conversely, claiming credit in a collaborative project requires explicit agreement in advance. If two researchers co-author a report or article, the nature of each contribution should be agreed before work begins. If a client provides documents that are essential to the research, credit the client's contribution in the report.

Sharing Research Online

Publishing family trees on platforms like Ancestry, WikiTree, and Geni creates de facto public records. The standard for shared online research is the same as for published work: every relationship should be supported by documented evidence; sources should be cited; and living individuals' privacy must be protected. Unsourced tree entries that are copied and propagated are the primary vector for genealogical error propagation — a significant professional concern.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old how genealogists check each other's work to make sure family trees are accurate — and what happens when a reviewer finds an error.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: You submit a proof argument to the NGSQ. The editor returns it with the following comments: (1) 'Your citation for the 1851 census entry is incomplete — you cite the family name but not the reference number.' (2) 'You have not addressed the possibility that the John Smith in the 1851 census is a different person from the John Smith in the baptism register — you need to eliminate this alternative.' (3) 'Your conclusion states this is "definite proof" — please revise to reflect the actual evidential standard.' How would you respond to each comment?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) The incomplete census citation is a straightforward error — look up the full TNA reference (piece, folio, page) for the specific entry and add it to the citation. Respond: 'Thank you for identifying this — I have corrected the citation to include the full piece and folio reference: [RG number]/[piece]/[folio]/[page].'

(2) The alternative identity concern is a substantive methodological issue. A proof argument must eliminate alternative explanations. Respond: 'I have added a section to the evidence analysis addressing this alternative. The case for identifying them as the same individual rests on: [specific corroborating evidence — consistent age in 1851 vs. baptism date; consistent geographic location; no other John Smith of consistent age found in the parish or adjacent parishes in the relevant census]. This is now explicit in the revised argument.'

(3) 'Definite proof' is inappropriate language — no genealogical conclusion warrants 'definite'. Respond: 'Agreed — I have revised the conclusion to read "The preponderance of the available evidence establishes with reasonable confidence that..." The original phrasing overclaimed the epistemic status of the conclusion.' This demonstrates engagement with the standard, not defensiveness about the criticism.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: You are reviewing a colleague's draft proof argument before she submits it to a genealogical journal. You notice: (1) she has used a family tree on Ancestry as her primary source for a claimed relationship between two 19th-century individuals; (2) her conclusion says the two individuals 'must be' related because of the DNA match; (3) she has not documented any searches that produced negative results. How would you frame your review comments to be constructive and professional, and what corrections would each comment recommend?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1) Ancestry family tree as primary source: Frame this constructively — not as a criticism of your colleague's ability but as a methodological gap that will likely be flagged by the journal editor. Comment: 'The Ancestry family tree you cite for this relationship would not meet NGSQ standards as a primary source — unsourced tree entries are derivative at best and may have errors. I recommend tracing the relationship through documentary records (birth/marriage/death certificates, census) to corroborate it independently before submission. The tree could be noted as a preliminary finding that prompted the documentary search.' Recommended correction: Document the relationship through original sources; use the tree only as a lead, not a citation.

(2) 'Must be related': DNA evidence shows a probabilistic relationship, not a certain one. Comment: 'DNA matching indicates a likely relationship within a cM range; it does not prove the specific relationship without documentary corroboration. "Must be related" overclaims. I suggest: "The DNA match of [X] cM is consistent with a [relationship range] and, combined with the documentary evidence of [specific finding], supports the conclusion that they were related as [stated relationship] with reasonable probability." The specific documentary corroboration is what elevates this from a DNA inference to a demonstrated conclusion.' Recommended correction: Revise language and add documentary corroboration.

(3) Missing negative evidence: Comment: 'The methodology section doesn't indicate which records were searched and found not to contain relevant information. This is required to demonstrate a reasonably exhaustive search (GPS Step 1). Please add a paragraph documenting which record series were searched and returned no relevant results — this strengthens the argument rather than weakening it.' Recommended correction: Add a negative results section documenting all searches conducted regardless of outcome.
learningObjectives: Identify the forms of peer review available to genealogical researchers and the standards each applies.
Demonstrate intellectual humility in responding to peer review — engaging with criticism constructively rather than defensively.
Apply effective peer reviewing principles: specific, constructive, focused on methodology not style.
Describe the ethical requirements for credit, attribution, and avoiding plagiarism in collaborative genealogical work.
commonMistakes: Treating peer review comments as personal criticism rather than as professional engagement with the work.
Responding to reviews defensively without checking whether the comment identifies a genuine methodological gap.
Providing vague peer review comments ('this needs more evidence') without identifying specific problems with specific citations or arguments.
Sharing research online without source citations, contributing to the propagation of genealogical errors through unsourced tree copying.
assessmentCriteria: Correctly identifies the types and purposes of peer review available to genealogists.
Demonstrates appropriate engagement with review comments — correcting genuine errors, explaining misunderstandings, making the case where the reviewer may be wrong.
Reviews others' work constructively and specifically, focusing on methodology and evidence rather than style.
Applies attribution and credit standards consistent with APG and BCG codes of ethics.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The National Genealogical Society Quarterly's editorial review process — submissions are reviewed by the editor and specialist reviewers against GPS standards before acceptance.
A free, collaborative genealogy platform that requires sources for all assertions and enforces a community-maintained quality standard — an attempt to address the unsourced-tree-propagation problem.
Multiple credentialled genealogists who independently review CG candidate portfolios; discrepancies between reviewers trigger discussion to ensure consistent standards.
A collaborative format used by genealogical societies in which a researcher presents a specific, unresolved research problem and invites collective problem-solving from fellow society members.

questions.questionHtml: What is the primary purpose of peer review in genealogical research?
options: To increase the researcher's publication record
To identify methodological gaps, citation errors, and unjustified conclusions before they are published and propagated
To give journal editors control over which research is published
To ensure all researchers use the same record sources
questions.correctAnswer: To identify methodological gaps, citation errors, and unjustified conclusions before they are published and propagated
questions.explanationHtml: Peer review provides a structured mechanism for catching errors in methodology, citation, evidence analysis, and conclusions before they enter the published record, where they may be copied and propagated by subsequent researchers.

questions.questionHtml: You are reviewing a colleague's proof argument and notice she has not addressed an obvious alternative explanation for the relationship she is arguing. How should you frame this comment?
options: 'This is wrong — you need to consider other possibilities.'

'The argument does not currently address the possibility that [specific alternative] — this is a gap that peer reviewers will flag. I recommend adding a section explicitly eliminating this alternative with reference to [specific evidence].'
'Your conclusion is probably correct, but just to be safe, add a note saying other possibilities exist.'
Leave it — it is not the reviewer's job to suggest improvements, only to note errors.
questions.correctAnswer: 'The argument does not currently address the possibility that [specific alternative] — this is a gap that peer reviewers will flag. I recommend adding a section explicitly eliminating this alternative with reference to [specific evidence].'
questions.explanationHtml: Effective peer review is specific and constructive: it names the exact issue, explains why it matters (GPS requires alternative explanations to be eliminated), and proposes a concrete correction. Vague criticism or silence are both unhelpful to the author.

questions.questionHtml: A colleague whose DNA project you have contributed to publishes findings that rely heavily on your analysis without mentioning your contribution. What is the appropriate professional response?
options: Accept it as normal — individual contributions to collaborative projects are not usually credited
Raise the issue directly with the colleague, citing the APG Code of Ethics requirement to properly attribute contributions, and request that an acknowledgement be added to any further publication
Publicly criticise the colleague on social media
Withdraw your contribution from the project and retract your analysis
questions.correctAnswer: Raise the issue directly with the colleague, citing the APG Code of Ethics requirement to properly attribute contributions, and request that an acknowledgement be added to any further publication
questions.explanationHtml: The APG Code of Ethics and the norms of scholarly collaboration require proper attribution of contributions. The appropriate first step is a direct, professional conversation with the colleague — not public criticism or unilateral action. Many attribution failures are oversights rather than deliberate plagiarism and can be corrected through direct communication.
